problem.approach: Compute the target r*unit, then walk the array keeping a running sum; the first index where the sum reaches the target is the answer.
problem.insight: A 'running sum until threshold' scan — the same skeleton solves fuel-station and minimum-houses style questions.
problem.inputFormat:
Line 1: r (number of rats).
Line 2: unit (units each rat eats).
Line 3: n (number of houses).
Line 4: n space-separated integers — food in each house in order.
problem.outputFormat: One integer: houses visited to reach the requirement, or 0 if impossible.
problem.solution:
r = int(input())
unit = int(input())
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
if n == 0:
    print(-1)
else:
    needed = r * unit
    total = 0
    count = 0
    for food in arr:
        total += food
        count += 1
        if total >= needed:
            print(count)
            break
    else:
        print(0)

problem.statement: r rats must collect food from houses arranged in a row. Each rat eats exactly `unit` units of food, so together they need r × unit units. Walking from the FIRST house onward, they collect all the food of each house they visit. Print how many HOUSES they must visit to gather at least the required food. If the total food in all houses is still not enough, print 0.
steps: Read r, unit, n and the array.
needed = r * unit — the total food requirement.
Walk the houses keeping total = food collected so far and count = houses visited.
The moment total >= needed, print count and stop — no need to visit further houses.
If the loop finishes without reaching the target, food is insufficient: print 0.
problem.title: Rat Count House

problem.learn: Full pipeline: JOIN -> GROUP BY -> HAVING (aggregate) -> ORDER BY.
problem.schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Customers(customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Orders(order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER); CREATE TABLE Payments(order_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER);
problem.seedSQL: INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ravi'),(3,'Meena'); INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (10,1),(11,1),(12,2),(13,3); INSERT INTO Payments VALUES (10,700),(11,500),(12,400),(13,2000);
problem.solution: SELECT c.name, SUM(p.amount) AS total_spent FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN Payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY c.name HAVING SUM(p.amount) > 1000 ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
problem.starter:
-- customers with total > 1000
SELECT c.name, SUM(p.amount) AS total_spent
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN Payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY c.name
HAVING SUM(p.amount) > 1000
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
problem.statement: Tables Customers(customer_id, name), Orders(order_id, customer_id), Payments(order_id, amount). Show name and total_spent for customers whose total exceeds 1000, ordered by total_spent desc.
steps: HAVING SUM > 1000 keeps Asha, Meena (WHERE SUM impossible).
ORDER BY total_spent DESC: Meena, Asha.
